learn.lesson: VWAP combines price and volume. Instead of treating every observed price equally, prices associated with more trading volume contribute more to the result. Intraday traders often compare current price with session VWAP as execution and market-location context.
commonMisconceptions: Price above VWAP does not guarantee that price will continue higher.
VWAP is a benchmark and descriptive statistic, not a standalone prediction.
warnings: Calculation conventions can vary by data source and price input.

advanced.definition: VWAP is a cumulative ratio of price-volume products to cumulative volume over the chosen interval.
advanced.methodology: For bar data, implementations commonly use a representative bar price multiplied by bar volume, accumulated through the session.
assumptions: The chosen price representation and session boundary are appropriate for the intended comparison.
limitations: VWAP is path-dependent within the chosen session and different session definitions can produce different values.

research.treatment: At research depth, VWAP should be treated both as a descriptive volume-weighted statistic and as an execution benchmark. Empirical work must specify data granularity, session boundaries, price construction, transaction-cost treatment and whether the research question concerns execution quality or predictive association.
empiricalQuestions: Does distance from VWAP have stable conditional information after costs in a specified market and regime?
methodologicalDebates: Tick-level versus bar-based reconstruction can change benchmark precision.

learn.lesson: P/E connects a stock price with earnings per share. A higher or lower P/E is not automatically good or bad: growth expectations, business quality, cyclicality, accounting choices and interest rates can affect comparisons.
commonMisconceptions: A low P/E does not by itself mean a stock is cheap.
P/E can be uninformative when earnings are negative or temporarily distorted.
warnings: Trailing and forward P/E use different earnings inputs.

advanced.definition: P/E is market price per share divided by earnings per share for a specified earnings period.
advanced.formula: P/E = Price per Share / Earnings per Share

variables.meaning: earnings per share for the specified period

limitations: Cross-company comparisons can be distorted by accounting, capital structure, cyclicality and differing growth expectations.

research.treatment: Research using P/E should define the earnings measure, measurement date, treatment of negative earnings, survivorship controls and comparison universe. Valuation ratios can be studied descriptively or as predictors, but predictive claims require out-of-sample evidence and cost-aware implementation.
empiricalQuestions: How stable are valuation relationships across sectors and rate regimes?
methodologicalDebates: Trailing, forward and normalized earnings can lead to materially different valuation conclusions.

learn.lesson: ATR describes recent price-range volatility. A $2 ATR has very different meaning for a $20 stock and a $500 stock, so traders often interpret it alongside price or use normalized variants.
commonMisconceptions: ATR does not indicate whether price will rise or fall.
warnings: ATR depends on lookback length and smoothing convention.

advanced.definition: ATR is a smoothed average of True Range, where True Range accounts for the current high-low range and gaps relative to the prior close.
limitations: ATR is scale-dependent unless normalized and is backward-looking.

research.treatment: Research should specify true-range construction, smoothing method, lookback, sampling frequency and normalization. ATR can serve as a volatility proxy, sizing input or regime feature, but any predictive use requires separate validation.
empiricalQuestions: How does ATR-based sizing affect drawdown and turnover after transaction costs?
methodologicalDebates: Alternative volatility estimators use different information and assumptions.

learn.lesson: In a short sale, securities are borrowed and sold, then equivalent securities must later be returned. Profit or loss depends on the repurchase price plus borrowing, trading and other applicable costs.
commonMisconceptions: A short position is not simply the mirror image of a long position because mechanics and risk differ.
warnings: Borrow availability and fees can change, and losses can grow substantially as price rises.

advanced.definition: A short position creates an obligation to return borrowed securities and produces mark-to-market exposure opposite a long position in the security, subject to financing, borrow and market-structure constraints.
advanced.methodology: Simulation must model sale proceeds, repurchase cost, borrow costs, transaction costs and position constraints rather than merely negating long returns.
limitations: Simplified simulators may understate real-world borrow scarcity, recalls, fees, margin requirements and execution constraints.

research.treatment: Short-sale research must account for borrow availability, borrow fees, delisting and survivorship effects, corporate actions, margin assumptions and asymmetric loss exposure. Backtests that assume every historical security was freely shortable can materially overstate implementability.
empiricalQuestions: How much simulated short-strategy performance survives realistic borrow and transaction-cost assumptions?
methodologicalDebates: Historical borrow data availability is a major limitation in many retrospective studies.

learn.lesson: The Sharpe ratio compares average return above a reference rate with return volatility. It is useful for summarizing one dimension of historical risk-adjusted performance, but it compresses a return distribution into a single statistic.
commonMisconceptions: A historical Sharpe ratio is not a probability of future success.
Two strategies with the same Sharpe ratio can have very different drawdowns and tail risks.
warnings: Sampling frequency, annualization and non-normal returns can materially affect interpretation.

advanced.definition: The Sharpe ratio is the mean excess return divided by the standard deviation of returns, with consistent periodicity and any annualization explicitly defined.
assumptions: Return observations and annualization conventions are appropriate for the inference being made.
limitations: Serial correlation, skewness, fat tails, estimation error and selection bias can make naive comparisons misleading.

research.treatment: Research-level use requires attention to estimator uncertainty, multiple testing, non-normality, serial correlation, changing regimes and selection bias. Report the sampling interval, annualization convention, reference rate and confidence/uncertainty rather than presenting Sharpe as an immutable property.
empiricalQuestions: How uncertain is the estimated Sharpe given sample size and dependence structure?
methodologicalDebates: Inference and annualization become less straightforward when returns are autocorrelated or non-normal.
